pois.name: Blakely Mountain Dam
pois.desc: Earth-and-rock-fill dam on the Ouachita River built by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. About 231 ft high and 1,100 ft long with its crest at 616 ft. The lake began filling in 1952–53; first power came in 1955 (2 units, 75 MW).

pois.name: Deepest point (modelled)
pois.desc: Lowest point of the reconstructed lake bed, in the old river channel just above the dam. The model is held to the Corps' original streambed elevation of 385 ft here, 193 ft below full pool.

pois.name: Pre-dam river gauge (1923–1950)
pois.desc: USGS gauge 07357000 measured the free-flowing Ouachita River for 27 years before the dam. Its gage datum was 404.16 ft, so the old riverbed here lay about 174 ft under today's full pool. Marker at the coordinates USGS lists for the site; the modelled channel passes about 1.4 km south, and the model is shallower than the documented datum at this exact spot.

pois.name: Buckville (submerged townsite)
pois.desc: A Garland County community inundated by the lake. Its church was moved in 1951; the cemetery stayed and is now reached by boat. Marker placed at the Buckville landing — the exact townsite is not documented.

pois.name: Buckville Cemetery
pois.desc: Listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Left in place when the valley flooded.

pois.name: Cedar Glades (submerged)
pois.desc: Former community covered by Lake Ouachita. Location from the GNIS place record.

pois.name: Ouachita River inflow
pois.desc: Where the Ouachita River enters the head of the lake's northwest arm. Upstream, at the USGS gauge near Mount Ida, the river drains 414 sq mi of the Ouachita Mountains.

pois.name: South Fork inflow
pois.desc: Head of the southwest arm, where the South Fork of the Ouachita River comes in.

pois.name: Quartz crystal veins form
pois.desc: Ouachita quartz grew from hot water in rock fractures about 280–245 million years ago.
pois.body: The quartz this area is famous for crystallised from hot, mineral-rich water that rose through fractures during the closing stages of the Ouachita mountain-building event, roughly 280 to 245 million years ago (Late Pennsylvanian to Permian). Radiometric dating of adularia, a feldspar that grew in some veins, supports that window. Most mined veins fill cracks in two Ordovician sandstones, the Crystal Mountain and Blakely sandstones, and the quartz belt runs about 30–40 miles long and 15 miles wide from near Little Rock to Oklahoma. Marker placed on the Crystal Mountains ridge (GNIS).

sources.t: Arkansas Geological Survey: Arkansas Quartz Crystals
Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Official State Mineral

pois.name: Washita
pois.desc: Montgomery County community near the head of the lake's Ouachita River arm.
pois.body: Washita is a small Montgomery County community near the head of the lake's northwest arm, where the Ouachita River comes in. 'Washita' is the phonetic spelling of 'Ouachita', the French rendering of a Native American name. East and West Washita cemeteries sit beside the settlement. Little of its history is documented in published sources; local records, family papers and photos are the best way to fill it in.

pois.name: Mount Ida
pois.desc: Montgomery County seat since 1842; known as the quartz crystal capital.
pois.body: Granville Whittington opened a post office here in June 1842 and named it Mount Ida after a hill near his former Massachusetts home. The county seat was first called Montgomery and briefly Salem (July 1850) before becoming Mount Ida in October 1850. The 'County House' log courthouse went up in 1846, and county records survive from July 1845. The Montgomery Hunters marched out to war on 17 July 1861, and Union troops held the town for several days in late 1863. Mount Ida incorporated on 30 May 1890 and had an all-woman city council in 1931–32. Lake Ouachita brought tourists in the 1950s; today it is billed as the Quartz Crystal Capital of the World.

pois.name: Montgomery County Courthouse
pois.desc: 1923 fieldstone courthouse; National Register of Historic Places, 1976.
pois.body: The current courthouse on Court Square was built in 1923 to a design by Clyde A. Ferrel. Its randomly laid fieldstone walls mix local rustic character with Classical Revival styling, including a pedimented entry with an oriel window. It replaced an 1873 frame building, which had replaced the 1846 log 'County House'. It holds the county's complete records from 1845 and was listed on the National Register in 1976.

pois.name: Cities Service Filling Station
pois.desc: Five-sided 1925 gas station on Whittington Street; NRHP 2001.
pois.body: Cities Service built this small five-sided station at 204 Whittington Street in 1925. Its hip roof extends into a canopy over the pumps on brick piers. It sold gas until 1966 and has since housed small businesses; it played a gas station again in the film White River Kid, shot here in 1998. National Register, 2001.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Mount Ida Cities Service Filling Station (CC BY-SA)

pois.name: Heritage House Museum
pois.desc: Free-admission museum of Montgomery County history.
pois.body: The Heritage House Museum of Montgomery County is a not-for-profit, free-admission museum in Mount Ida, and the best place to see local artifacts, photographs and family histories of the valley.

pois.name: Crystal mining
pois.desc: From a 1904 claim to WWII radio crystals to dig-your-own mines.
pois.body: Crystal hunting here was mostly unregulated until 1942. The first quartz mining claim came in 1904. In World War II, Ouachita quartz suitable for radio oscillators was found at Fisher Mountain, and a quartz-buying office opened in Hot Springs in 1943. Synthetic crystals ended most industrial demand after the war. Production reached about 44,000 lb in 1987, and industrial lascas mining continued to 1997. Arkansas made quartz crystal its state mineral in 1967, and the World Championship Quartz Crystal Dig is held here each October. Today, fee mines let visitors dig and keep what they find. Marker at Wegner Crystal Mines (OSM).

sources.t: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Official State Mineral
Encyclopedia of Arkansas: World Championship Quartz Crystal Dig

pois.name: Silver City boom (1876–1882)
pois.desc: An 1880s silver rush brought 1,000+ people; every mine had closed by 1882.
pois.body: Lead and silver prospecting began before 1840 near Gap Creek. From 1874–75, miners from Colorado and California drifted in, and by 1880 the crossroads called Silver City reportedly had over 1,000 people. Hundreds of claims were worked, about three dozen shipped ore, and by the end of 1882 every mine had closed. The best known were the Minnesota, owned by riverboat magnate 'Diamond Jo' Reynolds, and the Walnut, owned by Joplin, Missouri's 'Lead King' Elliott Moffet. A brief revival followed the 1888 Bear gold rush, which turned out to be a fraud by crooked assayers. Marker at the GNIS place 'Silver'; the exact townsite is not confirmed.

pois.name: Fir (vanished community)
pois.desc: Big Fir and Little Fir died out; their names live on as lake recreation areas.
pois.body: GNIS lists 'Fir (historical)' here. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas notes that the Big Fir and Little Fir communities died out as farms and lumber companies sold land to the national forest, then came back as popular Lake Ouachita recreation areas. Big Fir and Little Fir cemeteries are still mapped near the lake (OpenStreetMap).

pois.name: Oakwood (Chalybeate Spring)
pois.desc: Listed among the communities lost to Lake Ouachita.
pois.body: A Montgomery County history page lists Oakwood, also called Chalybeate Spring, with Old Buckville, Cedar Glades, Flea Bend and White Plains as communities under Lake Ouachita. GNIS places the historical Oakwood at the head of the north arm, beside today's Oakwood Cemetery and Mount Zion Church, so parts of the old community may have been above the waterline. 'Chalybeate' means iron-bearing spring water.

sources.t: ARGenWeb Montgomery County: Blakely Mountain Dam

pois.name: Murphy Cemetery
pois.desc: Graves moved up from the valley floor before the flood were reburied here.
pois.body: The Corps of Engineers' 1951 'Relocation Plan of Cemeteries' for the Blakely Mountain Reservoir records 518 graves removed from sixteen cemeteries and reburied at Murphy Cemetery, about 14 miles east of Mount Ida near US 270. Relocations ran in mid-1952 as the gates closed. Family accounts note that some markers were never moved and that only recent graves were fully exhumed.

pois.name: Mauldin (ghost town)
pois.desc: Logging town of 300 that was dismantled and hauled away by rail in 1937.
pois.body: The Caddo River Lumber Company's railroad reached the Mauldin logging camp in the early 1920s, making it the county's logging centre. In 1936 a commissary and post office served about 300 people. In 1937, almost overnight, the town was dismantled and carried off by rail as the company pulled up its tracks; the virgin timber was gone. Much of the cut-over land became Ouachita National Forest.

pois.name: Guinn Dipping Vat
pois.desc: c.1940 concrete cattle-dipping vat from the fight against Texas tick fever; NRHP 2006.
pois.body: Mack Guinn built this U-shaped concrete vat around 1940 so local farmers could dip cattle to kill the ticks that spread Texas tick fever. It sits in the ghost town of Mauldin, south of Forest Road 37, and was listed on the National Register in 2006.

pois.name: Womble District Administration House
pois.desc: CCC-built c.1940 ranger headquarters on US 270; NRHP 1993.
pois.body: A Civilian Conservation Corps crew built this one-and-a-half-floor frame house about 1940 as headquarters of the national forest's Womble District, on US 270 just west of Williams Stream. Theodore Roosevelt created the Arkansas National Forest in 1907; it was renamed the Ouachita National Forest in 1926, and 63% of the county eventually became forest land. National Register, 1993.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Womble District Administration House No. 1 (CC BY-SA)

pois.name: CCC Company 741 powder magazines
pois.desc: Explosives stores of Arkansas's first CCC camp, c.1936; NRHP 2007.
pois.body: Camp 741 of the Civilian Conservation Corps, the first CCC camp established in Arkansas, built these two stone-and-concrete magazines around 1936 to store explosives for road and bridge building. The main magazine is 8 × 16 ft; the blasting-cap store is about 113 m to its northwest, off Forest Road 177M.

sources.t: Wikipedia: CCC Company 741 Powder Magazine Historic District (CC BY-SA)

pois.name: Collier Springs Shelter
pois.desc: 1939 CCC stone-and-log shelter built over a spring.
pois.body: CCC crews built this open stone shelter with hewn log beams in 1939. It covers the spring itself, which is piped to the nearby creek. It is one of the CCC works in the county listed on the National Register.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Collier Springs Picnic Area (CC BY-SA)

pois.name: Womble Trail
pois.desc: 37-mile IMBA Epic singletrack along the Ouachita River bluffs.
pois.body: This Forest Service singletrack runs more than 37 miles from North Fork Lake to the Ouachita National Recreation Trail, partly along bluffs above the Ouachita River. It is open to hikers and mountain bikers (no horses), marked with white triangles, and rated an IMBA Epic for about 6,000 ft of climbing.

pois.name: 13,500 years in the Ouachita valley
pois.desc: People lived in this valley for some 13,500 years before the lake; traces lie beneath the water.
pois.body: Before Blakely Mountain Dam, rural communities such as Buckville, Avant and Cedar Glades grew up in the Ouachita River valley between the 1880s and 1950. Beneath the lake are traces of much older communities: places where Native people lived over the past 13,500 years. That history is known from oral traditions, from explorers' written accounts, and from archaeology. Archaeological sites at Lake Ouachita are protected under federal historic preservation law; please do not dig into sites or remove artifacts. This marker shows the general area only; archaeological sites are protected and are not mapped.

sources.t: Arkansas Archeological Survey: Indian History in the Lake Ouachita Region (M. B. Trubitt)

pois.name: Ice Age hunters: Clovis and Dalton
pois.desc: A quartz-crystal Clovis spear point was found during Blakely Mountain Dam construction.
pois.body: The earliest artifacts from this area date to the Paleoindian period, about 11,500–10,500 BC, when people across North America hunted mammoth, mastodon and bison with Clovis-tipped spears. Distinctive Clovis and Dalton points show small groups living in the Lake Ouachita region near the end of the Ice Age; Dalton hunters relied on deer as the climate changed. A Clovis point chipped from quartz crystal was discovered during construction of Blakely Mountain Dam (Arkansas Archeological Survey, Sargent Collection; described by Julie Morrow in 2002). Marker near the dam, where the source says it was found; no exact findspot is given.

sources.t: Arkansas Archeological Survey: Indian History in the Lake Ouachita Region (M. B. Trubitt)
Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Montgomery County (Dalton culture)

pois.name: Archaic river life and novaculite trade
pois.desc: Net fishing, hickory nuts and novaculite tools traded as far as Louisiana and Mississippi.
pois.body: Rich game, fish and plants drew people to the Ouachita River valley. In the Middle Archaic, riverside settlements may have been lived in year-round. Notched pebble net weights show net fishing, especially in spring and early summer when catfish, gar, buffalo and largemouth bass gathered to spawn. Hickory nuts were a key food: archaeologists find nut-cracking anvil stones and charred nutshell on Archaic sites here. Novaculite, a hard, fine-grained stone like chert, was the preferred toolstone of the Ouachita Mountains. It was quarried from ridge-top outcrops, leaving pits, trenches and debris piles that are among the largest archaeological sites in Arkansas, many protected in the Ouachita National Forest and Hot Springs National Park. Novaculite tools reached Louisiana and Mississippi through long-distance trade, especially in the Middle and Late Archaic, about 6000–1000 BC. This marker shows the general area only; archaeological sites are protected and are not mapped.

sources.t: Arkansas Archeological Survey: Indian History in the Lake Ouachita Region (M. B. Trubitt)

pois.name: Fourche Maline villages (Woodland period)
pois.desc: Woodland-period pottery makers, studied at the Poole site before the lake flooded it.
pois.body: Between about 1000 BC and AD 1000, people of the Fourche Maline culture (named for a creek in eastern Oklahoma) lived in the Lake Ouachita region; they were probably ancestral to the later Caddo. The Poole site, excavated by WPA crews before the lake was built, shows Fourche Maline communities making pottery and chipping dart points and tools from local stone, and a pattern of wall posts read as a long rectangular house. Native crops such as goosefoot, squash and sunflower likely supplemented hunting, fishing and gathering. Squash from recent excavations in Montgomery County is radiocarbon dated to AD 715–940, an early clue to farming in the Ouachita River valley. This marker shows the general area only; archaeological sites are protected and are not mapped.

sources.t: Arkansas Archeological Survey: Indian History in the Lake Ouachita Region (M. B. Trubitt)

pois.name: Caddo farming villages and the Adair mounds
pois.desc: Caddo farmers grew maize, squash and beans here; a Caddo mound center now lies under the lake.
pois.body: Caddo people were farmers. In Caddo oral tradition, the first Caddo woman came up onto the earth carrying corn and pumpkin seeds. Archaeologists find Caddo farming villages along the Ouachita River, with charred maize, squash, beans and goosefoot on sites dating from the 1300s to 1600s. The Adair site, a Caddo mound center excavated by WPA crews in 1939, now lies under Lake Ouachita. Crews mapped several mounds there, one 14 ft high; a trench through it showed a series of burned and rebuilt buildings, and elsewhere they found the posts of large circular houses and a cemetery area. Caddo communities were usually farmsteads spread out around a mound center, with thatched round houses that early observers likened to beehives. This marker shows the general area only; archaeological sites are protected and are not mapped.

sources.t: Arkansas Archeological Survey: Indian History in the Lake Ouachita Region (M. B. Trubitt)

pois.name: What was for supper, 600 years ago
pois.desc: Deer, turkey, fish, turtles, river mussels and hickory nuts, from excavations in the national forest.
pois.body: Excavations in the Ouachita National Forest have recovered animal bone, mussel shell and charred nuts and seeds from old refuse pits. Caddo people living here about 600 years ago hunted deer, turkeys, rabbits and squirrels with bows and arrows (earlier people used spears), caught turtles and fish, collected mussels from the Ouachita River, and gathered large quantities of nuts. Survey researchers have published foodways results from 2013–14 excavations at a Montgomery County site. This marker shows the general area only; archaeological sites are protected and are not mapped.

sources.t: Arkansas Archeological Society, Ouachita Chapter: What's for Supper? Native American Foods in the Ouachita Mountains
Arkansas Archeological Survey: Indian History in the Lake Ouachita Region (M. B. Trubitt)

pois.name: Removal, and the Caddo Nation today
pois.desc: The 1835 treaty took Caddo land in Arkansas; the Caddo Nation's government is in Oklahoma today.
pois.body: Caddo people enter written history with the de Soto–Moscoso expedition in 1542. By the time settlers reached the Ouachita River in the early 1800s, no Native people were living in the valley. The final loss of Caddo homelands in Arkansas came in 1835, when Caddo headmen were coerced into signing a treaty ceding all Caddo land, never again to live there as a group. After a long journey, the Caddo Nation's seat of government is now in Caddo County, Oklahoma, five miles east of Binger, where the Caddo Heritage Museum is located. In 2006 the federally recognized Caddo Nation of Oklahoma listed 4,774 members, all lineal descendants of the ancient Caddo Nation. Caddo names remain on Arkansas maps, and Caddo people remember these homelands.

sources.t: Arkansas Archeological Survey: Indian History in the Lake Ouachita Region (M. B. Trubitt)
